entries.meaning: The mothers properly worship gods and ancestors and fulfil every cherished wish, bowing to all and asking only that Rāma and his brothers remain blessed. Invisible gods give benedictions, which the delighted mothers gather into the folds of their garments. Daśaratha summons the wedding guests and gives them vehicles, clothing, gems and ornaments; holding Rāma in their hearts, they return happily home. Every man and woman in the city receives clothing, music and congratulations fill every house, and the king gives each petitioner exactly what is asked, fully rewarding servants and musicians. Then he returns home with guru and Brahmins.

Daśaratha reverently follows every instruction Vasiṣṭha gives, whether social or Vedic. Seeing the crowd of Brahmins, the queens rise and count themselves fortunate; feet are washed, guests bathed, worshipped, fed by the king, enriched with honour, gifts and love, and sent away satisfied while bestowing blessings. Daśaratha worships Viśvāmitra in many ways, declaring none as blessed as himself, praises him greatly, and with the queens takes the dust of his feet. He gives the sage a fine inner lodging and the women’s palace watches over him with care, then worships the guru’s lotus feet again as king, queens, sons and brides repeatedly bow and receive blessings.

With deep love Daśaratha places his sons and wealth before the guru and makes a humble offering. The sage accepts the customary gift, grants many blessings, embraces Rāma and Sītā in his heart, and joyfully returns to his dwelling. The king summons Brahmin women, clothes and ornaments them, then gives married women garments chosen to their taste. Every ritual recipient receives a fitting gift, and all dear, honoured guests are properly respected. Having seen Raghubīra’s wedding, the gods praise the celebration, shower flowers, sound drums and return delighted to their own worlds, telling Rāma’s glory to one another.

After satisfying and dismissing everyone according to custom, Daśaratha goes to the women’s palace, his heart still overflowing. He sees the princes with their brides, takes the sons into his lap in delight, and lovingly seats and fondles each bride. Joy takes up residence in every heart. The queens ask how the marriage happened, and Daśaratha recounts the whole story; they rejoice to hear him praise Janaka’s character, affection, customs and lovely wealth in the manner of a court bard. After bathing with his sons, the king calls Brahmins, guru and kin to an elaborate meal; five watches of night have passed.

Noble women sing auspicious songs through the beautiful night, root of happiness. Everyone receives betel after rinsing and glows adorned with garlands, fragrance and ornaments. With the king’s leave they bow to Rāma and return home, while love, delight, playful celebration and the loveliness of the gathering continue to grow beyond the descriptive power of Sarasvatī, Śeṣa, Veda, Brahmā, Śiva or Gaṇeśa. Daśaratha honours all, gently tells the queens that the young brides have come to an unfamiliar home and should be guarded like eyelids protect the eyes, and asks that the tired, sleepy children be put to bed. He retires with his mind at Rāma’s feet.

At the king’s word the mothers spread gem-set golden beds with soft, lovely mattresses white as fragrant milk foam, fine pillows, garlands, perfumes, jewelled chambers, lamps and canopies beyond description. They prepare Rāma’s couch, raise him lovingly and lay him down, then repeatedly direct the other brothers to their own beds. Gazing upon Rāma’s tender dark body, they affectionately ask how he travelled the terrifying road, killed Tāṭakā, and overcame the fierce night-roamers Mārīca and Subāhu with all their helpers as though no warriors counted at all.

The mothers credit the sage’s grace for their dear son’s power: he warded off many divine dangers, guarded the sacrifice with his brother, learned every science from the guru, and freed the sage’s wife Ahalyā with the dust of his feet, filling the worlds with fame. He broke Śiva’s bow, harder than a thunderbolt upon the tortoise’s back, in the gathered court, won world-famous Jānakī, and returned home with all four brothers married. Such superhuman deeds were accomplished only through Kauśika’s grace. Their lives are fulfilled by seeing his moon-face; may Brahmā not count the days spent without him. Rāma gently satisfies them, remembers Śiva, guru and Brahmins, and closes his eyes in sleep.

words: I offer myself in loving admiration

entries.meaning: Rāma’s sleeping face is exquisitely lovely, like a golden lotus at dusk. In every house women keep a festive vigil and exchange affectionate wedding taunts. Ayodhyā shines through the night; queens urge companions to behold the lovely brides sleeping beside their mothers-in-law, like crest-jewels hidden in female serpents’ hearts. At sacred dawn the Lord wakes as fine red-crested cocks call. Bards sing virtues and townspeople salute at the gate. All four brothers bow to Brahmins, gods, guru, father and mother, receive blessings, complete purification and bathe in the holy river, then finish morning rites and approach their father.

Daśaratha embraces his sons and happily seats them with permission. The whole assembly is refreshed by seeing Rāma and counts the sight the highest gain of the eyes. Vasiṣṭha and Kauśika arrive and receive fine seats; the king and sons worship and bow, while both gurus gaze at Rāma with love. Vasiṣṭha relates histories of dharma to the king and women’s palace, then joyfully tells at length Viśvāmitra’s deeds, unfathomable even to sages. Vāmadeva confirms every word and says the adorned fame has spread through all three worlds. Thus each day passes in auspicious joy as Ayodhyā’s bliss continually swells.

On a propitious day the wedding bracelets are ceremonially removed amid abundant joy and play. The gods envy Ayodhyā’s ever-new happiness and ask Brahmā for birth there. Viśvāmitra daily wishes to depart, but Rāma’s loving courtesy holds him; seeing Daśaratha’s affection grow a hundredfold each day, the great sage praises it. When he finally asks leave, the king stands before him with sons and says all his wealth, family and self belong to the sage; he begs continuing affection for the boys and future visits. King, queens and sons fall at his feet speechless. After many blessings Kauśika departs, with Rāma and the brothers escorting him until commanded home, while he inwardly praises Rāma, the king’s devotion and the wedding joy.
